title: How I program my Squat days for Natural Hypertrophy
summary: His two squat days, skewed toward hamstrings because his quads and glutes are already big and past knee injuries call for a balanced leg. He squats heavy only once every 8 days. The big quad day is high-bar squats, front squats and pause squats, supersetted with grip, lat and core work. The second day is hamstring-biased: box front squats, front rack holds, hip thrusts, SSB good mornings and an RDL giant set.

claims.claim: His squat days are about 35% hamstrings and 65% quads, and his deadlift days 90% hamstrings and 10% quads, as part of his plan to reach 28-inch legs naturally.
Squats mainly build the quads but also heavily involve the glutes, hamstrings, hips and lower back.
Big quads aren't a good thing in his case: past sports knee injuries mean too much quad relative to posterior chain creates imbalances that can cause knee problems, especially tendinitis.
Developed quads do take some strain off the knee, but the whole leg needs developing, so his leg training is skewed toward hamstrings; his glutes are already big.
He squats heavy only once every 8 days but does knee-flexion work every leg day, using variations that bias the hamstrings over the quads.
His big squat day opens with high-bar squats (he dislikes low bar and thinks high bar looks better) for 1-3 heavy sets of 4-8 reps.
Front squats are his favorite squat variation even though they don't suit his build; he does 3 sets of 4-5 relatively heavy reps.
He front squats about 3 plates and back squats about 3.5 plates; front squatting almost as much as he back squats shows how quad-dominant he is.
He always supersets front squats with hanging leg raises plus 'strength restoration' band work for thoracic extension, spine health and elbow mobility.
He does pause squats ass-to-grass for 4-8 reps at about 80% of his max (around 300 lbs), supersetted with grippers, strength restoration and towel grip.
Squats don't involve the forearms or lats, so he uses squat rest periods for extra forearm work and close-grip pull-ups.
Calf work on squat day is piano raises and Toshiki raises with close-grip pull-ups between sets, letting calves rest while training the lats.
He often ends the big squat day with a nonstop giant set of close-grip pull-ups, knee raises and strength restoration until burnt out, then leg raise ab work.
He trains in sub-zero temperatures and his knees take 35-40 minutes to warm up for heavy squats, so squatting daily or every 3-4 days doesn't work for him.
Nothing taxes his recovery more than squats, more than deadlifts, so heavy squatting every 8 days works for him.
His second squat day starts with front squats to a parallel box, then front rack holds, an Olympic accessory for core, upper back and thoracic extension strength to stay upright.
He does high-rep hip thrusts with a foot placement that targets the hamstrings.
He does safety squat bar good mornings in a way that targets the hamstrings, since he doesn't want more lower back or glute size.
His second squat day ends with a 6-round no-rest giant set of Romanian deadlifts, grippers, barbell hyperextensions, grip tools and strength restoration, then ab training.
He deadlifts two days after squatting, so his leg days complement each other.

exercises.why: main quad builder; looks better than low bar to him

exercises.name: Box front squat to parallel
exercises.why: lighter quad work on the hamstring day
